wording: Original paraphrase. POST ids follow the order of the source list; text is not the source text.
refs_source: OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 (github.com/OWASP/ASVS/tree/v5.0.0), checked 2026-10-16. "V8.4" names a section or chapter; "8.2.1" names one requirement.

trigger_vocabulary.dependencies: Adds, updates or vets libraries, starters, vendors or managed services.
trigger_vocabulary.accounts: Sign-in, sessions, passwords, recovery or user roles.
trigger_vocabulary.multitenant: More than one user, company or organization whose data must stay separate.
trigger_vocabulary.enterprise: Contract, procurement or security-review requirements from larger buyers.
trigger_vocabulary.database: Persistent data, schema, migrations or data lifecycle.
trigger_vocabulary.payments: Charges, subscriptions, invoices, tax, refunds or usage billing.
trigger_vocabulary.ai: Model calls, agents, prompts, tools or AI-generated actions.
trigger_vocabulary.jobs: Background, scheduled, retried or queued work.
trigger_vocabulary.regulated: Health, financial, children or other specially regulated data.
trigger_vocabulary.privacy: Personal data, retention, deletion, residency or policy promises.
trigger_vocabulary.children: Product may be used by or collect data from minors.
trigger_vocabulary.integrations: Third-party APIs, webhooks or OAuth connections.
trigger_vocabulary.public-api: A customer-facing API or integration surface.
trigger_vocabulary.frontend: User interface, forms, localization or accessibility.
trigger_vocabulary.deploy: Shipping, hosting, environments, pipelines or configuration.
trigger_vocabulary.ops: Running a live service: monitoring, incidents, cost, recovery.
trigger_vocabulary.scale: Meaningful traffic, data volume or latency pressure.
trigger_vocabulary.org: Several people run or support the product, or customers and contracts expect formal operations (on-call, status page, staff tools).
trigger_vocabulary.distribution: App stores, offline sync, device permissions or hardware.

controls.concern: Data model designed deliberately up front, not accreted table by table by an AI.
Sign-in works with unusual but valid email forms such as plus-addressing.
Password-reset links are single-use and expire.
Multi-factor authentication with a recovery route for users who lose their device.
Sessions expire, and all sessions for one account can be revoked.
Single sign-on for customers whose contracts require it.
SAML support where a customer actually requires that protocol.
SCIM provisioning so offboarding in a customer directory removes access promptly.
Role and permission model richer than admin versus everyone else.
Object-level checks so one user cannot read another user's records by editing an identifier.
Tenant isolation so one customer's data never appears for another.
Support impersonation, only if needed, with an audit record of every use.
Rate limiting on sign-in to resist large-scale password guessing.
Lockout rules that slow attackers without stranding legitimate users.
Schema migrations that apply cleanly and have a tested recovery path.
Migrations that avoid long locks on busy tables.
Indexes chosen so queries stay fast at realistic data volumes.
Connection pooling so traffic spikes do not exhaust the database.
Regular automated backups.
Backups proven by an actual restore test, not just a configured schedule.
Point-in-time recovery for accidental mass deletes or updates.
Recoverable deletion so an accidental removal is a support request, not an incident.
Validation enforced on the server, not only in the form.
Times stored and displayed correctly across time zones.
Names with apostrophes and other punctuation work end to end.
Emoji, accented characters and right-to-left text work in every input.
Money held in exact units, never binary floating point.
Currency, rounding and tax rules for each market sold into.
Data model that tolerates a customer's changing requirements.
Idempotency keys so a retried payment cannot charge twice.
Protection against duplicate submissions from repeated clicks.
Pagination that still works on very deep pages.
Data export for customers who ask for their records.
Imports tolerate messy or legacy-format files.
Retention rules, with code that deletes what contracts and policy promise.
Secrets kept out of code, repositories and AI chat history.
Rotate any key an AI tool previously placed in configuration or chat.
Every installed package confirmed to exist and be the one intended.
Dependency vulnerability scanning, with review of newly added libraries.
Untrusted input handled safely wherever users can type or paste content.
Protection against injection, cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery and other common web weaknesses.
Uploaded files checked, size-limited and stored where they cannot execute.
Cross-origin rules configured narrowly instead of open to everyone.
Security headers on responses.
Encryption in transit and at rest.
Least-privilege access for people and AI agents, especially any holding production credentials.
Activity logs attributing actions to people while excluding credentials, tokens and card data.
Independent penetration test before an enterprise buyer runs their own.
Evidence-backed answers to buyers' security questionnaires.
A process for receiving and handling outside vulnerability reports.
Response plan for a lost or stolen device that has production access.
SOC 2 treated as a scoped audit program with policies and evidence, not a checklist.
HIPAA applicability assessed as soon as patient-related records may be handled.
Business associate agreements with vendors, including model providers, where HIPAA applies.
Audit trails showing who viewed a record, not only who changed it.
Card-data scope understood and raw card numbers kept out of your database.
Privacy-rights deletion requests handled across data stores, logs and backups per a stated policy.
Data residency honored where a contract restricts location.
Periodic access reviews with named sign-off.
Development, staging and production kept consistent with each other.
Infrastructure defined as code rather than in one person's memory.
Deploy pipeline runs tests before anything reaches customers.
Fast rollback or roll-forward after a bad release.
Deploys that do not cause customer-visible downtime.
Feature flags to separate shipping code from releasing a feature.
Autoscaling for predictable load spikes.
Content delivery network so distant users get fast loads.
DNS and certificates renewed well before expiry.
Background queues so slow work does not block the interface.
Retries with backoff so a transient failure does not lose work.
Dead-letter handling for jobs that exhaust their retries.
Scheduled jobs that do not run twice when another server is added.
Caching with correct invalidation when data changes.
SPF, DKIM and DMARC so transactional mail is not filed as spam.
Bounce and complaint handling for transactional email.
Storage lifecycle rules so stale files stop accruing cost.
Cost alerts that surface runaway spend the same day.
Written disaster-recovery plan, exercised periodically.
Second region only if a contractual uptime promise requires it.
Structured logs that can be searched during an incident.
Error tracking that groups repeats of the same defect.
Uptime checks that run from outside your own network.
Alerts that page a human and are tuned to avoid noise.
Operational dashboards covering response time, failure rate and request volume.
Tracing a slow request across every service it touches.
An on-call arrangement with a named person who responds.
Runbooks explaining what each alert condition means and what to do.
Postmortems that lead to changes.
Customer-facing status page.
Unit tests derived from the stated intended behavior, each shown to fail when that behavior breaks.
Integration tests for each third-party API relied on.
Full-journey tests covering signup, checkout and the other flows the business depends on for revenue.
Load testing before launch, against an approved non-production target.
Realistic test data that is not real production data.
Regression tests so fixing one bug does not revive an old one.
Testing on the older hardware and browsers key customers actually use.
Accessibility conformance where a contract or law requires it.
Subscriptions, plan changes and proration.
Failed-payment retries and dunning communication.
Invoices carrying buyer reference numbers such as purchase-order numbers.
Sales tax and VAT handling.
Refund, credit and partial-refund handling.
Usage metering that reconciles exactly with billed amounts.
Billing logic that can accommodate custom annual contract terms.
Revenue reports finance can reconcile.
Inbound webhooks verify signatures.
Outbound webhooks retry and keep a record of failed deliveries.
Versioned API so changes do not break customer integrations.
Customer-managed API keys that can be issued and revoked.
API rate limits that protect the service without blocking legitimate integrations.
A plan for when a third-party API changes its responses unannounced.
OAuth token refresh handled before and after expiry.
Sandbox where customers can test their integration.
Prompt-injection defenses for every input that can reach a model.
Sensitive data kept out of prompts unless sent to an approved, properly configured processor.
Per-customer model spend caps.
Evaluations that reveal when a model update degrades answers.
Fallback behavior for a model-provider outage.
Migration plan for when a model is deprecated.
Prompt and output logs for debugging, excluding anything not permitted to be kept.
Human approval before any irreversible action the AI takes.
Pages that load acceptably on slow networks.
Empty, loading and error states on every screen.
Error messages a customer can act on.
Forms keep what people typed when validation fails.
Emails render correctly in the mail clients your customers use.
Notifications users can turn off.
Undo where it is practical.
Keyboard navigation and screen-reader support.
Translations with locale-appropriate dates and numbers.
Back-button behavior that matches expectations.
Code a maintainer can read and follow.
Every change reviewed against its diff before release, with the reviewer recorded; a self-review is labeled as one.
Branching strategy that lets several people work without overwriting each other.
Regular dependency upgrades so the project never falls far behind.
Framework upgrades before the old version loses security support.
Dead code left behind by earlier attempts removed.
Overgrown files split into coherent modules.
Architecture decisions written down with reasons.
README that gets a new developer running locally quickly.
Documentation for whoever inherits the project.
Admin panel for the operations team.
Internal tools that let customer-facing staff resolve questions without involving engineers.
Changelog customers can read.
Terms and privacy policy that match what the code actually does.
Accounts, domains and repositories owned by the organization, not an individual builder.
More than one person able to maintain the system.
Lane: a senior engineer reads all AI-written code before it ships.
Lane: a backend engineer designs the data model before growth exposes its flaws.
Lane: a senior engineer can explain why a fix introduced new defects.
Lane: an operations owner for deploys, rollback, servers and cloud spend.
Lane: a named person answers production alerts such as a payment outage.
Lane: security patches framework vulnerabilities quickly after disclosure.
Lane: security/compliance can walk an auditor through how sensitive data moves.
Lane: QA independently verifies what the AI claims it tested.
Lane: a backend owner runs live migrations without losing data.
Lane: a tech lead declines features that destabilize others.
Lane: an architect makes it work for all customers at once, not one laptop.
Lane: a senior engineer can debug when the AI that wrote the code cannot.
Lane: someone preserves the reasons the system is built this way.
Write a scoped threat model, trust boundaries, abuse cases and accountable risk decisions.
Test race conditions and atomicity for inventory, permissions, quotas and payments.
Handle SSRF and network egress restrictions for URL fetchers, webhooks and AI tools.
Protect software supply chains with provenance checks, pinned dependencies and reviewed install scripts.
Confirm open-source licenses, attribution and commercial obligations before reuse.
Define measurable service objectives, recovery point and recovery time objectives, then rehearse them.
Check preview deployments and staging for unintended public exposure and production credentials.
Model consent, data minimization, lawful processing and children-related restrictions where applicable.
Define per-environment configuration validation and safe failure on missing critical settings.
Exercise graceful degradation, timeouts, cancellation and circuit breaking for unavailable dependencies.
Document upstream update strategy and exit/export paths for managed services and starter forks.
Validate distribution-specific requirements such as app-store permissions, offline sync or hardware safety when applicable.
Restrict field-level reads and writes by permission so clients cannot set or see fields they do not own (mass assignment).
Enforce authorization on the server for every request, deny by default, including exports, background jobs and admin routes.
Take the tenant from the authenticated session, never from client input, and scope every query, cache, search index, file path and export by it.
Gate admin and support functions behind a separate permission and recent re-authentication, and audit each use.
Write the authorization rules per role and resource and test them as a permission matrix with negative cases.
Accept uploads only by content inspection plus extension, with per-file size and per-user count limits.
Store uploads under server-generated names outside the web root; never use a user-supplied file name as a path.
Serve downloads with a safe content type, attachment disposition and nosniff, through links scoped to the owner that expire.
Bound archive and image processing against decompression bombs and parser exploits, and isolate that processing.
